docs.title: Interpretation Board
docs.text:
Mohammed Al Rasbi | Team 105 | RAS 304

Our project is a handheld LiDAR device intended to help visually impaired users notice nearby obstacles through sound and vibration. The enclosure is inspired by a portal gun. My interpretation board receives range information from the data-collection board and controls a warning speaker and a small vibration motor in the grip.

docs.title: My contribution
docs.text:
I am responsible for the interpretation controller, audio output, vibration output, and their local power circuitry. The main motor that rotates the LiDAR belongs to the scanning subsystem.

docs.title: Current design
docs.text:
The design uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, PAM8302 speaker amplifier, DRV2605L vibration driver, and a local 5 V regulator. The documentation follows simplified schematic revision D-simple.

Current figures are estimates and controller settings are proposed. Hardware testing and an actual MCC project have not been completed. Team UART levels, data format, and available supply current still need confirmation.

Team 105 project website

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Mohammed Al Rasbi - Interpretation Board

My board receives LiDAR data from Khun's collection board, interprets obstacle information, and provides speaker and vibration alerts. The vibration motor sits in the grip. The main LiDAR rotation motor belongs to the scanning subsystem.

Figure 1: Current interpretation subsystem, matching simplified schematic D-simple.

docs.title: Connections and design decisions
docs.text:
Interface Connection Power Proposed 9-12 V from Jose through fuse, diode and local 7805 regulator. The Nano and both driver modules use 5 V. Data input Khun TX to J2 pin 1, then Nano RC3/RX, pin 8. J2 pin 8 is common GND. Optional data output Nano RC2/TX, pin 7, to J3 pin 1. Destination remains unassigned; leave unused unless needed. J3 pin 8 is GND. Speaker RB0 PWM through the filter to PAM8302; RB3 controls shutdown. Speaker connects across amplifier outputs. Vibration RB1/SCL and RB2/SDA connect to DRV2605L. Configure the driver for the 3 V ERM motor.

Pins 2-7 on J2 and J3 are unused. All boards need a common ground and compatible UART signal voltage; confirm the collection board's levels before integration.

The controller separates range processing from the higher-current actuators. Audio and vibration offer two nonvisual feedback methods. Local regulation supplies the electronics, while the driver modules power the loads. This revision replaces the original PWM motor-driver proposal with I2C and matches the separate UART input/output headers in the schematic.

docs.title: Audio amplifier
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: Adafruit 2130 - PAM8302A module$3.95 eachProduct link - One channel matches the required warning speaker.- Small module and input trim simplify assembly and level adjustment. - Needs analog audio conditioning from PWM.- Available output can exceed the selected speaker rating; limit drive. Option 2: Adafruit 987 - MAX98306 module$8.95 eachProduct link - Selectable gain provides useful volume headroom.- Two channels allow a later left/right audio experiment. - Second channel is unnecessary in this design.- Higher price than the mono option; speaker power still needs limiting. Option 3: Adafruit 1552 - TPA2012 module$9.95 eachProduct link - Gain switches simplify prototype tuning.- Built-in protection and analog inputs suit a breadboard prototype. - Costs more than the selected mono module.- Unused stereo channel and short-speaker-wire guidance complicate packaging.

Choice: Adafruit 2130 / PAM8302A

Rationale: The PAM8302A is compact, inexpensive, and provides the single audio channel needed for warning tones. Its volume trim makes adjustment easier; filter and attenuate the PIC PWM signal and keep output within the speaker rating.

Product photos and specifications: linked supplier pages.

docs.title: Speaker
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: Adafruit 3923 - mini oval$1.95 eachProduct link - Compact shape fits a handheld body.- 1 W rating offers more margin than the mini metal option. - Supplier page currently says out of stock.- Short lead and enclosure opening require mechanical planning. Option 2: Adafruit 1890 - mini metal$1.95 eachProduct link - Small, shallow package is easy to place.- Attached wires simplify prototype connections. - Lower continuous rating requires stricter volume limiting.- Listed out of stock; title and detailed power ratings differ, so use 0.25 W rated. Option 3: Adafruit 1313 - 3-inch speaker$1.95 eachProduct link - Mounting tabs provide a secure attachment method.- Compatible impedance and power class for the mono amplifier. - Large diameter and depth consume handheld space.- Heavier than the oval option and currently listed out of stock.

Choice: Adafruit 3923 mini oval speaker

Rationale: The oval speaker fits the handheld enclosure better than the larger round option and has a higher power rating than the mini metal speaker. It is the preferred design choice, but its listed stock shortage must be resolved before ordering.

Product photos and specifications: linked supplier pages.

docs.title: Vibration motor driver
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: Adafruit 2305 - DRV2605L$7.95 eachProduct link - Built-in effects help distinguish warning states.- Two I2C signals reduce timing work in the PIC. - Requires register initialization and motor calibration/settings.- Costs more than the generic H-bridge and changes the earlier PWM interface. Option 2: Adafruit 3297 - DRV8833$5.95 eachProduct link - Low-voltage operation suits a roughly 3 V motor.- Protection and current-limiting capability simplify experiments. - No built-in haptic effect sequencing.- Second bridge is unused; default current limit is far above this small motor load. Option 3: Adafruit 2448 - TB6612$6.95 eachProduct link - Separate motor and logic rails can suit larger actuators.- Supports direction and speed control with standard digital signals. - Supplier recommends 4.5-13.5 V motors; poor fit for the selected 3 V ERM.- Extra control pins and unused bridge add complexity; rejected for this design.

Choice: Adafruit 2305 / TI DRV2605L

Rationale: The DRV2605L provides built-in vibration effects and reduces the software needed to create distinct alerts. Use I2C instead of the earlier PWM-only interface and configure the driver for the selected ERM motor.

Product photos and specifications: linked supplier pages.

docs.title: Vibration motor
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: Adafruit 1201 - vibrating disc$1.95 eachProduct link - Enclosed mechanism avoids exposed rotating mass.- Low price and compact disc suit grip mounting. - Requires a driver and controlled motor voltage.- Mounting stiffness strongly affects feedback; supplier sheet/model consistency needs checking. Option 2: Pololu 1637 - shaftless 8 mm$6.95 eachProduct link - Smaller diameter fits a narrow grip.- Adhesive backing and specified startup current aid integration. - Higher price than the selected disc.- Supplier shows backorder availability; smaller force needs grip testing. Option 3: Pololu 2265 - cylindrical ERM$6.95 eachProduct link - Flat-sided sleeve helps secure the motor.- Narrow profile can fit along the grip wall. - Exposed eccentric mass needs clearance.- Backorder availability and higher price make it less attractive.

Choice: Adafruit 1201 vibrating disc

Rationale: The enclosed disc is small, inexpensive, and easy to mount inside the grip. Drive it through the DRV2605L at a nominal 3 V motor setting, then test the strength of the vibration in the enclosure.

Product photos and specifications: linked supplier pages.

docs.title: Local power regulation
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1: Adafruit 2164 - 7805 TO-220$0.75 eachProduct link - Through-hole package is practical for a custom student PCB.- Low unit cost and fixed output avoid adjustment errors. - Needs input headroom, capacitors and thermal design.- Heat reduces battery efficiency; verify actual manufacturer/marking before purchase. Option 2: Adafruit 184 - MIC2941 kit$14.95 eachProduct link - Lower dropout increases input-voltage flexibility.- Kit includes heatsink and prototyping connections. - Large assembled kit and higher cost hurt handheld integration.- Listed out of stock; linear heat loss remains despite lower dropout. Option 3: Pololu 5433 - D45V5F5$5.75 eachProduct link - Switching conversion can reduce battery losses.- Very small board with simple VIN/GND/VOUT connections. - Switching-only solution does not meet the stated linear-regulator direction.- Current capability depends on input and temperature; rejected as sole local regulator.

Choice: 7805-based local linear regulator circuit

Rationale: The 7805 is inexpensive, easy to solder, and supports the required local linear-regulator approach. The current schematic assumes a 9-12 V input from Jose. Confirm the voltage under load and use the power budget to size the heatsink.

Product photos and specifications: linked supplier pages.

docs.title: Controller and product requirements
docs.text:
The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano provides the controller and programming interface for this subsystem. The speaker and vibration motor support nonvisual obstacle alerts, and the small modules fit the handheld concept. The DRV2605L uses I2C; the rotating LiDAR motor is not driven by this board.

The selected Adafruit 2305 is the QT revision with onboard I2C pull-ups. The amplifier and haptic module are powered from the local 5 V rail. The motor's nominal 3 V setting is configured in the driver. The speaker power target for the estimated budget is 0.25 W, below its 1 W rating.

docs.title: Proposed MCC configuration
docs.text:
Planning configuration only. An MCC project has not been generated or tested. Match these signals in the PIC18F57Q43 MCC pin manager and verify peripheral pin selection before generating code.

Function PIC port Nano connector pin Proposed configuration UART receive from collection board RC3 8 UART RX, digital input; proposed 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit. Agree with Khun. Optional UART forwarding RC2 7 UART TX, digital output; same framing. No destination assigned yet. Haptic clock RB1 10 I2C SCL, proposed 100 kHz, open-drain configuration. Haptic data RB2 9 I2C SDA, bidirectional/open-drain configuration. Audio output RB0 46 PWM output; proposed carrier at least 62.5 kHz with audio duty-cycle modulation. Amplifier enable RB3 47 Digital output, start low to mute amplifier. Status LED RD0 20 Digital output, start low. Board power VTG 51 External regulated 5 V. Disable onboard regulator VOFF 55 Grounded in the schematic. Ground GND 15, 24, 33, 42, 52 Common ground.

Propose a 32 MHz internal system clock and a timer for alert scheduling. Disable analog input mode on digital signal pins. Configure UART, I2C, PWM and GPIO through MCC, checking that each selected peripheral can route to the required pin. The ADC is not required by this design. Leave the board's USB VBUS carrier pin unused.

Initialize the DRV2605L at I2C address 0x5A for the 3 V ERM motor and calibrate it. Receive and validate range packets, choose an alert state, then update audio and vibration. Detect missing or invalid data separately from a clear path; timeout and distance thresholds must be agreed and tested.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Mohammed Al Rasbi - Interpretation Board

The controller receives LiDAR data and converts obstacle information into sound and vibration. This gives the user feedback without needing to look at a screen.

Figure 1: Simplified interpretation-board schematic, revision D-simple.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Power: J1 accepts a proposed 9-12 V input from Jose's power board. F1 and D1 protect the input; U1 produces 5 V for the Nano and driver modules. Capacitors reduce supply disturbances. U1 requires a heatsink.
  • Controller: U2 is the complete PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano. Its firmware will interpret incoming range information and select warning patterns. Pin numbers refer to the Nano board connector.
  • Data input: J2 pin 1 receives Khun's TX signal and connects to RC3/RX, Nano pin 8. J2 pin 8 is common ground.
  • Optional data output: RC2/TX, Nano pin 7, connects to J3 pin 1. No receiving board is assigned yet; leave J3 unconnected unless the team needs forwarding. J3 pin 8 is ground. Pins 2-7 on both UART headers are unused.
  • Sound: RB0 supplies PWM audio through R4/R5/C8/R6/C9 to the PAM8302 amplifier. RB3 enables the amplifier. The speaker connects across OUT+ and OUT-, with neither lead connected to ground. The power estimate assumes a reduced 0.25 W audio target, which must be checked by measurement.
  • Vibration: RB1/SCL and RB2/SDA command the DRV2605L over I2C. Its two output leads drive the grip motor. Configure it for the selected 3 V ERM motor; the driver itself receives 5 V.
  • Status: RD0 drives the status LED through R1.

Audio and tactile outputs provide two feedback methods. Compact modules simplify assembly inside the handheld enclosure. The simplified design omits the previous debug button, expansion header, test points and isolation jumpers.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Mohammed Al Rasbi - Interpretation Board

This estimated budget uses the course spreadsheet template and the simplified schematic. It assumes simultaneous sound and vibration. These are planning allowances, not measured currents or guaranteed maximum ratings.

docs.title: Estimated 5 V loads
docs.text: Load Current allowance Basis Curiosity Nano, GPIO and status LED 80 mA Board-level allowance including control-pin loads; measure at the selected clock. PAM8302 and speaker 70 mA 0.25 W audio / (5 V x 80% assumed efficiency), plus 7.5 mA overhead. DRV2605L and vibration motor 100 mA Combined input allowance; verify startup and selected vibration effects. Subtotal 250 mA Speaker and motor are included in their driver rows, not counted twice. Including 25% margin 312.5 mA 250 x 1.25.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The 312.5 mA estimate leaves 37.5 mA below the proposed 350 mA continuous regulator design allowance. That allowance depends on adequate heatsinking; it is not a tested regulator limit.

Adding an estimated 8 mA regulator ground current gives approximately 320.5 mA from the shared input. At 12 V input, regulator dissipation is approximately 2.28 W: (12 - 5) x 0.3125 + 12 x 0.008. This conservatively ignores the series diode's voltage drop in the regulator calculation. The diode also produces heat.

The budget shows why a heatsink and limited speaker power matter. At a 1 W speaker output, the same assumptions would require approximately 547 mA on the 5 V rail including margin, exceeding the 350 mA design allowance. Test the output level and adjust the design if louder alerts are needed.

Jose's available current allocation, shared battery capacity and full-team load are not confirmed. Source margin and battery runtime therefore remain TBD. The 500 mA fuse is protection, not proof that startup current or thermal performance is acceptable.
